methodology: Publicly accessible article text was read. No paywalls were bypassed. A paid label does not necessarily mean the lead case study is inaccessible; these records distinguish accessible lead sections from locked material. Numerical claims retain their original unit, time window, and evidence type. Newsletter analysis is not Valve telemetry or a causal experiment.

sources.name: The GameDiscoverCo newsletter
sources.author: Simon Carless
sources.strongestUse: Game-by-game launch timelines, creator and showcase discovery, player overlap, and estimated wishlist trajectories; frequent direct developer data.
sources.blindSpots: Mixes disclosed numbers with proprietary estimates. Hit-focused case selection. Some charts and full analyses require Plus or Pro; newsletter access is not a dataset license.
sources.access: Free articles and public lead sections; paid newsletter and Pro platform also offered

sources.name: Game Marketing Intel
sources.author: Cole
sources.strongestUse: Readable Next Fest cohort comparisons, follower-based wishlist estimates, small-game marketing tactics, and templates.
sources.blindSpots: Author describes himself as a solo developer/pharmacist rather than a Valve insider. Wishlist proxies, incomplete polling and excluded age-gated titles can alter conclusions. Treat algorithm explanations as hypotheses.

sources.name: The Alinea Insight newsletter
sources.author: Rhys Elliott / Alinea Analytics
sources.strongestUse: Cross-platform unit/revenue estimates, wishlist-to-buyer cohorts, regional distribution, audience overlap, and pricing context.
sources.blindSpots: Estimates are not publisher accounts. Overlap is not incremental attribution. Public articles show selected outputs rather than the complete model or dataset; rhetoric can be stronger than evidence.
sources.access: Free newsletter; commercial analytics platform and client material

sources.name: OP Game Marketing
sources.author: Jordan Brown, Frostbloom co-founder
sources.strongestUse: Niche scans with downloadable cohorts and marketing mini-cases, especially taverns, productivity games and turn-based hybrids.
sources.blindSpots: Often uses Gamalytic estimates and handpicked cohorts. Filtering out low-revenue or 'non-serious' games inflates apparent hit rates; publisher relationships are relevant context.
sources.access: Public articles and linked research sheets

sources.name: GameDev Reports
sources.author: Dmitriy Byshonkov
sources.strongestUse: Finding original industry reports, regional market data and newly announced game milestones; a high-coverage research inbox.
sources.blindSpots: Not independent confirmation of its upstream sources. Forecasts, publisher announcements and model estimates have different definitions. Follow original links before using a number in a decision.
sources.access: Public summaries; paid reports archive and premium updates

sources.name: Butterscotch Shenanigans development blog
sources.author: Sam, Seth and Adam Coster / studio team
sources.strongestUse: Actual project chronology, experiments, wishlist CSVs, production constraints, unsuccessful channels and commercial results.
sources.blindSpots: A 14-year studio's accumulated team and pipeline advantages do not transfer to a new team. First-party attribution remains observational. Irregular publication; not a market-wide panel.

sources.name: Push to Talk
sources.author: Ryan K. Rigney
sources.strongestUse: Positioning, audience psychology, marketing craft and candid creator interviews, including commercial disappointments.
sources.blindSpots: Irregular schedule; not a current Steam sales database. Historical market figures must retain their year. Author's current a16z marketing role and earlier live-service background are context.
sources.access: Public archive; some subscription content may vary

sources.name: Game File
sources.author: Stephen Totilo
sources.strongestUse: Developer interviews, platform changes, business reporting and checking the circumstances behind headline successes or failures.
sources.blindSpots: Not a Steam niche-demand estimator. Many reports require subscription. Archive checked; no inaccessible article was treated as read.

articles.title: Hearth & Hamlet’s ~100k & the rise of the bite-sized clicker...
articles.author: Simon Carless
relatedGames: Sir, We Have an Orc Problem
articles.summary: A solo teacher's compact city-themed incremental illustrates demand for finite, low-friction progression. The city-builder appearance also attracted players expecting manual construction, which the fixed-layout design did not provide.
hardData: Headline reports approximately 100k copies; game was nine days old.
Publisher supplied >200k launch wishlists and 7h20 median playtime.
Price cited: $8; Steam review sentiment: 79% positive.
Publisher region split: US 23%, China 14.5%, Germany 13%.
articles.evidenceType: Publisher-disclosed case data plus analyst interpretation
articles.actionableLesson: Make the upgrade fantasy visually obvious, keep scope finite, and explicitly show whether construction is authored or player-directed.
articles.limitations: No full cost disclosure or controlled channel attribution. Forecast revenue is not earned revenue; omitted here.
articles.access: Public lead case study; later weekly charts are paywalled

articles.title: How have the genres of hit PC games changed since 2021?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: A comparison of top-five genre tags among commercially successful 2021 and 2025 releases shows a shift toward run-based hybrids, life simulation and idlers. Both unit- and revenue-based views are provided.
hardData: >50k-unit cohorts: 261 games in 2021 versus 469 in 2025.
Their median current US prices: $19.99 versus $16.99.
>$1m-gross cohorts: 196 versus 311 games.
2025 unit-cohort rank changes: Roguelite +39 to #1; Life Sim +31 to #6; Idler +46 to #15.
articles.evidenceType: GameDiscoverCo model estimates and tag analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Compare both copies and revenue; use a rising tag to locate comparables, not as a design brief.
articles.limitations: Winner-only cohorts do not measure success probability or supply. Tags overlap; prices are current, not necessarily launch prices.

articles.title: Will Big Walk’s 1m+ sales usher in a ‘co-op only’ game era?
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Big Walk expands social co-op beyond chaos into a shared journey of communication and discovery. A strong reveal and later gameplay showcase generated interest without a public demo.
hardData: Panic confirmed 1m paid copies across platforms in approximately six days.
Steam peak cited: 46k CCU; estimated launch wishlists: almost 1m.
2023 Game Awards reveal rapidly passed 100k estimated wishlists.
GDCo Steam overlap estimates: PEAK 75%, Lethal Company 67%, Untitled Goose Game 6%.
articles.evidenceType: Publisher milestone plus analyst estimates
articles.actionableLesson: Design moments that require friends to talk; target the social co-op audience rather than assuming the studio's previous audience transfers.
articles.limitations: Development began around 2020; established developer and publisher. Multi-platform sales and subscription players are separate measures.
articles.access: Public lead case study; later weekly charts are paywalled

articles.title: How Iron Nest sold >250k copies in less than 3 days...
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Tactile controls, mechanical sound and a confined artillery fantasy made raw clips compelling. Mission variety reused one environment. Short video created early attention; playtests, longer videos and the demo broadened the funnel.
hardData: Two developers; just over one year of development.
Developer data as of day five: >365k copies, $4.7m gross, 4% refunds.
>400k wishlists before the demo; >700k Next Fest demo players.
Demo later reached 876k players with 2h19 median playtime.
articles.evidenceType: Developer-disclosed results and interview
articles.actionableLesson: Concentrate art and audio on one satisfying machine, then create missions by recombining procedures instead of building more maps.
articles.limitations: Not a three-week completed-game comparator. Inspired by PVKK; the article discusses differentiation and shipping-speed concerns.
articles.access: Public lead case study; later weekly charts are paywalled

articles.title: Putting your game in a showcase? 5 key Qs to ask...
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: Showcase selection should consider lineup size, co-streaming, reveal density, cost, duration and audience fit. The article links event appearances to estimated wishlist movement rather than claiming every showcase works.
hardData: GDCo tracked 385 showcases overall, including 68 in its leading-event group since July 2024.
Typical lineups cited: 35–40 games at Triple-I versus roughly 60–70 at some large shows.
Tears of Metal: estimated >150k units since July 22; demo ranked #9 of 2,966 in October 2025 Next Fest.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst estimates and event inventory
articles.actionableLesson: Before paying, request audience, co-streaming and comparable-game results; use a genuinely new reveal and a ready Steam page.
articles.limitations: Seven-day wishlist gains are estimated, confounded by other campaigns and unavailable for games lacking a Steam page.

articles.title: How Guildrun genre-mashed its way to ~300k demo players in 10 days
articles.author: Simon Carless
articles.summary: A PvE autochess/roguelike hybrid found players asking for that exact combination. Months of weekly balance iteration and specialist creator coverage preceded a same-day reveal and demo launch. Short-form was not a major driver.
hardData: >275k demo players; 3h55 median playtime; 25% exceeded ten hours.
Approximately 230k wishlists by July 27; demo peak 14k CCU.
Discord grew from 250 early testers to 3k at demo launch.
Team included six full-time staff alongside founders, freelancers and outreach support.
articles.evidenceType: Developer-disclosed data and interview
articles.actionableLesson: Search niche communities for an unmet mode request, then validate with specialists and balance telemetry before mass promotion.
articles.limitations: Paid creators and ads were also used. Strong craft, experience and funding; not evidence that all acquisition was organic.

articles.title: What actually predicts Next Fest success?
articles.author: Cole
articles.summary: A broad June Next Fest scrape finds pre-existing interest and real demo engagement associated with better results. Starting wishlist totals were more correlated with gains than recent velocity in this dataset.
hardData: Approximately 279 games lacked wishlist estimates and were excluded.
80% of demos did not reach ten concurrent players.
Estimated median wishlist gain rose from 224 in the 1–9 CCU bucket to 1,284 in the next bucket.
The 2k–5k starting-wishlist cohort was the first with median gains above 1k.
articles.evidenceType: Follower-derived estimates and observational cohort analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Release the demo early enough to fix feedback; monitor natural engagement, not manufactured concurrent sessions.
articles.limitations: Wishlist proxy was adjusted during the event; pre-event CCU polling was incomplete. Correlation is not an algorithm threshold.

articles.title: How many of the 4,000+ games in Next Fest are you actually competing with?
articles.author: Cole
articles.summary: The relevant competitive set is narrower than the total festival catalog. Filtering by genre and evidence of existing interest reveals a more useful comparison group, while weak demand in a small genre remains a warning.
hardData: 4,350 participating games at the initial snapshot; 175 excluded for inaccessible follower data.
1,241 of 4,175 had <100 estimated wishlists; 2,146 had 100–2k; 788 exceeded 2k.
Point-and-click cohort: 272 games, only 27 above 2k estimated wishlists.
General wishlist proxy used: followers ×12.
articles.evidenceType: Steam API scrape plus wishlist proxy
articles.actionableLesson: Benchmark against comparable games with a real audience, while retaining the low-performing cohort to understand risk.
articles.limitations: Calling only high-interest games competition is an interpretation. Proxy and age-gate exclusions affect counts; tags are non-exclusive.

articles.title: Steam completely changed Popular Upcoming - here's what you need to know
articles.author: Cole
articles.summary: Early analysis of the June storefront redesign distinguishes the more selective Popular Upcoming widget from personalized calendar discovery. Historical wishlist rules of thumb no longer describe the same placement.
hardData: Homepage beta began April 1; public rollout cited as June 4, 2026.
Article reports the Personal Calendar can surface games approximately two months before launch.
articles.evidenceType: Observed platform change plus analyst interpretation
articles.actionableLesson: Use current Steamworks documentation and actual traffic-source reports; do not plan launch around an old 7k-wishlist promise.
articles.limitations: Early observations, not Valve's ranking specification. Reported entry ranges are not fixed or guaranteed thresholds.

articles.title: Another ''friendslop'' challenger enters the Steam arena
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: A failing-airline co-op fantasy generated substantial pre-release demand through short social clips. The analyst connects low price friction and audience circulation among co-op games, while warning about incoming clones.
hardData: Article reports >1m Dear Passengers wishlists and no paid marketing, creators or ads to that point.
Alinea estimates: 48% of wishlisters own R.E.P.O.; 47% PEAK.
Estimated R.E.P.O. prelaunch-wishlist conversion: 38% by day seven, 64% by day thirty.
Developer Flexus is a roughly 70-person studio, not a tiny new team.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst estimates and reported campaign information
articles.actionableLesson: Test a shared everyday role under absurd pressure; evaluate group purchase friction and regional pricing before choosing a price.
articles.limitations: Pre-release demand is not sales. Selected successful co-op conversions do not establish a universal rate; studio resources matter.

articles.title: Mortal Shell 2 passed half-a-million sold in its first weekend
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: Two very different releases show the need to separate audience fit, pricing and demo evidence. How to Fish combined inexpensive co-op with familiar social audiences; Mortal Shell 2 attracted many players new to the original.
hardData: Alinea estimate: How to Fish 1.9m units, approaching $8m revenue; launch price $4.95.
How to Fish overlap: PEAK 53%, Content Warning 27%.
Mortal Shell 2: estimated 510k multi-platform units and $23m revenue; 57.6% of units on Steam.
Approximately 600k Steam demo players; 9% of Steam buyers had played the original.
articles.evidenceType: Alinea model estimates
articles.actionableLesson: Keep platform and regional splits explicit; investigate demo engagement and relevant audience overlap instead of relying on franchise familiarity.
articles.limitations: No causal proof that demos drove purchases. Landfall financially supported How to Fish; it is not an unsupported zero-budget comparator.

articles.title: Steam Next Fest's winners, and why the event might matter less than you think
articles.author: Rhys Elliott
articles.summary: The piece argues Next Fest amplifies demand rather than creating it. Bombanana's legible asymmetric co-op premise snowballed through creators; Nightwater used an incentivized Bongo Cat collaboration, a distinctly different acquisition route.
hardData: Bombanana page launched 25 days before Next Fest after approximately five months' development.
A creator tweet reached approximately 650k views; 60% of demo players exceeded one hour.
Over the Hill: estimated >400k demo players, roughly 100k event wishlists.
Nightwater: approximately 75k event wishlists; 73% of wishlisters played Bongo Cat that month.
articles.evidenceType: Analyst estimates plus developer campaign account
articles.actionableLesson: Label incentive-driven wishlists separately. Prepare an independently attractive demo and creator campaign rather than relying on festival inclusion.
articles.limitations: Wishlist conversion uses different cohorts and time windows. Strong claims about event causality are interpretation, not controlled evidence.

articles.title: Newzoo: The Gaming Market in 2026 - powered by Mellow
articles.author: Dmitriy Byshonkov
articles.summary: A digest of Newzoo's updated global forecast places PC growth in context. It explicitly explains why estimates from providers can disagree when off-store spending and geographic coverage differ.
hardData: Newzoo forecast: global software/services spending $213.9bn in 2026, +6.1% year on year.
PC forecast: $45.9bn, +5.3%; 977m PC players.
2025 PC growth was revised to 12%.
Full Newzoo report was scheduled for September 10, after this research cutoff.
articles.evidenceType: Secondary summary of analyst forecast
articles.actionableLesson: Use PC-specific and region-specific measures; never treat global games spending as the addressable market for a Steam niche.
articles.limitations: Forecast, not final 2026 actuals. Covers software/services beyond Steam and excludes tax, hardware, advertising and gambling.
articles.access: Public digest; upstream report availability varies

articles.title: Games and Numbers (August 12 — August 25, 2026) - powered by Mellow
articles.author: Dmitriy Byshonkov
articles.summary: A useful index of original milestone announcements across platforms. It puts fast breakout stories beside Arco's much slower recovery, and distinguishes free player acquisition from paid unit sales.
hardData: Machine Party: >1m copies in two weeks, linked to its Steam announcement.
ReStory: >300k copies in a week and $3m gross by August 10, linked to Steam.

Arco: >100k worldwide copies across platforms and development-cost breakeven after two years, confirmed to Game Developer on August 18, 2026. Available on Steam, Nintendo Switch, Mac App Store and Epic Games Store; most sales came through Steam, but no exact Steam unit count was disclosed.
Moonlighter: >7m free additions in five days; these are not paid sales.
articles.evidenceType: Aggregator linking publisher disclosures and reporting
articles.actionableLesson: Use this as a lead finder, then open the original announcement and record paid/free, platform scope and elapsed time.
articles.limitations: Different underlying evidence types; these figures are not independently audited by the newsletter. Milestones overrepresent winners. Arco's cross-platform milestone must not be labeled Steam-only.

articles.title: How Well Do Turn Based Combat Games Perform on Steam?
articles.author: Jordan Brown
articles.summary: A large turn-based-combat cohort shows a severe mean/median gap. The author studies hybrid loops, presentation, pricing and co-op, but the filtered observational sample cannot identify which design choice causes success.
hardData: 1,542 games released since January 2023; snapshot August 13, 2026.
Estimated median gross revenue $7,744 versus average $776,940.
Top 1% took 69.4% of revenue; top 10% took 95.8%.
Games under $500 estimated revenue and NSFW/unreleased titles were excluded.
articles.evidenceType: Steam/Gamalytic estimated cohort analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Look at median and downside cases before adding a strategy genre to the shortlist; identify a second appealing loop and production cost.
articles.limitations: Co-op, price and art correlations are confounded by budget and team quality. Exclusions make the apparent success rate optimistic.
articles.access: Public article and linked full cohort sheet

articles.title: How Tavern Games Are Quietly Printing Money on Steam
articles.author: Jordan Brown
articles.summary: A tavern theme supports several distinct audiences: cozy management, chaotic co-op, narrative and horror. Mini-cases describe free entry, demos, creator outreach, paid short-form testing and post-launch content.
hardData: Handpicked sample: 38 titles, 22 released.
12/22 released games estimated above $100k gross; 7/22 above $1m.
Median price $14.99.
Bronzebeard's Tavern was a five-person student project and free; Ale & Tale had a four-person developer team.
articles.evidenceType: Gamalytic estimates and selected campaign mini-cases
articles.actionableLesson: Choose the player fantasy within the theme, then validate with the corresponding creators; do not mistake 'tavern' for a single genre.
articles.limitations: Outside priority window. Excludes NSFW and subjectively weak contenders; 12/22 is not the probability a new tavern game succeeds.
articles.access: Public article and linked cohort sheet

articles.title: The Rise of Productivity Games on Steam
articles.author: Jordan Brown
articles.summary: A narrow productivity cohort separates focus companions, customization-driven work rewards, social accountability and parasocial companionship. Marketing sells the feeling of getting work done, not just a timer and a feature list.
hardData: 34 selected games; data collected February 5–6, 2026.
Nine had >500 reviews; three had estimated gross revenue >$1m.
Virtual Cottage 2 had 58,026 estimated wishlists.
Pure idle and bottom-of-screen games were excluded.
articles.evidenceType: Steam/Gamalytic estimates and qualitative positioning analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Define a specific work ritual and audience; test cozy lifestyle creators, customization sharing and relevant cross-promotions.
articles.limitations: Outside priority window; small handpicked cohort and estimated numbers. Review counts alone do not establish profitability.
articles.access: Public article and linked cohort sheet

articles.title: How Wyldheart Secured Over 200k Wishlists in 1 Month.
articles.author: Jordan Brown
articles.summary: A coordinated reveal combined a PAX East presentation, press embargo, creators, trailer and Kickstarter. The lesson is orchestration, not that unknown teams should hide their work for years.
hardData: March 27 reveal; >200k wishlists and >4k Discord members within one month.
Kickstarter raised €272,214 from 5,869 backers against a €150k goal.
Studio was founded in 2020 with industry veterans; article cites >$7.9m funding.
Closed backer beta began May 15.
articles.evidenceType: Public campaign records and practitioner analysis
articles.actionableLesson: Coordinate genuinely complementary announcement assets and embargoes; only use a late reveal when a strong playable and distribution relationships already exist.
articles.limitations: Outside priority window. Veteran, funded team is unlike a three-week micro-team. Campaign spending and attribution are not fully disclosed.

articles.title: Indie Dev Timeline for How Many Dudes
articles.author: Sam Coster and Seth Coster
articles.summary: A first-party timeline contrasts an expensive, long project with a fast-to-understand, replayable game. It exposes experiments and actual wishlist history rather than retroactively reducing success to a single viral moment.
hardData: July 30, 2026 launch, exactly one year after the idea.
173k Steam units sold in the first week.
The studio had fourteen years of prior experience.
A downloadable annotated wishlist CSV accompanies the article.
articles.evidenceType: First-party developer account and underlying CSV
articles.actionableLesson: Keep your own dated experiment log: hook, asset, channel, cost, baseline, observed change, and alternative explanations.
articles.limitations: One successful studio case, not a typical outcome. Accumulated experience and pipeline matter; not a one-year beginner benchmark.
articles.access: Public full developer blog and linked CSV; not a Substack

articles.title: Are Old Games Killing New Games?
articles.author: Ryan K. Rigney, interview with Antonio Uribe
articles.summary: An interview with Arco's co-creator demonstrates that strong reviews and a respected publisher do not guarantee sufficient launch revenue. The marketer also describes initially misreading its visual presentation as a slow narrative game.
hardData: Arco had 98% positive Steam reviews at the article's snapshot.
The developer said first-month income did not fund six months of team work.
Interview describes 197 main encounters plus sixteen arena encounters.
articles.evidenceType: Direct developer interview; historical snapshot
articles.actionableLesson: Check whether screenshots and the first seconds of a trailer communicate the actual play experience; include admired commercial underperformers in comparisons.
articles.limitations: Historical counter-case, not 2026 market data. Playtime-share figures in the original concern 2023 and are not used as current estimates.

agreements.point: A familiar loop plus a legible fantasy or visible twist is easier to communicate than a feature list.
A festival is one amplification moment in a longer funnel. Preparing a playable demo and attracting the right people beforehand are repeatedly present in successful cases.
Low-priced social co-op and finite incrementals show strong demand signals, but the same success stories frequently involve experienced teams, publishers, funding or months of iteration.
Niche audiences matter more than broad platform labels: PvE autochess, tactile machinery, social co-working and tavern management have different creators and reasons to buy.

disagreementsAndResolution.positions: Game Marketing Intel's broad proxy-based June sample finds starting wishlist stock more correlated with gains; Chris Zukowski's July 14 self-reported sample finds momentum modestly stronger.
disagreementsAndResolution.resolution: Different samples and estimation methods can produce both findings. Track both; neither proves Steam's ranking formula. Do not delay all marketing to manufacture a last-minute spike.

disagreementsAndResolution.positions: Alinea's June article is skeptical about wishlist-to-sale conversion, yet its July co-op analysis shows strong conversion for selected inexpensive games. Other practitioners use wishlists as intent benchmarks.
disagreementsAndResolution.resolution: Keep cohort, price, acquisition source and conversion window. Intent matters, but a wishlist is not a purchase and no universal conversion factor is justified.

disagreementsAndResolution.topic: Is short-form always the best channel?
disagreementsAndResolution.positions: Iron Nest and Dear Passengers gained early short-form traction; Guildrun explicitly did not.
disagreementsAndResolution.resolution: Use visual spectacle and immediately readable social failure for short-form; use specialist long-form for strategy depth. Test channel fit per game.

disagreementsAndResolution.positions: Cheap co-op/incremental cases convert well; the turn-based analysis favors longer, higher-priced games.
disagreementsAndResolution.resolution: Price is part of positioning and production scope. Cross-genre correlations are not a pricing experiment; use relevant comparables and a viable budget.

disagreementsAndResolution.topic: Do high niche hit rates establish an opportunity?
disagreementsAndResolution.positions: Selected tavern and productivity cohorts look encouraging; the broader turn-based cohort shows extreme concentration.
disagreementsAndResolution.resolution: Retain denominator and exclusions. Use curated success cases to generate hypotheses, then add weak launches, unreleased supply and production costs before committing.
